segments.say: You wake up, and for a moment you are certain it happened. Your heart is racing, your breath is short, and your mind is still holding the last scene as if it were a memory from yesterday. Then the room comes into focus, the ceiling is where it always is, and you realise that none of it was real. Nothing happened at all.

Here is what's strange about that moment. While it was going on, you didn't doubt it for a second. You didn't think, this seems unlikely, or, I wonder whether I'm dreaming. You simply believed it, and you felt every bit of it, the fear, the relief, the sudden longing, with a body that responded as though it were all true.

So tonight, let's take our time with this one. Find a comfortable place, let your shoulders drop, and let the voice be a quiet companion in the background. There's no rush, and nothing you need to remember. If you drift off along the way, that's perfectly fine. The ideas will still be here when you come back.

Here's the road we'll walk together tonight. We'll begin with the night scientists discovered that sleep has a hidden second life. Then we'll look at what your brain is doing while you dream, and why you accept the strangest scenes without a flicker of doubt. We'll find out why you lie still, how sounds and smells sneak into the story, and what people really dream about. And near the end, we'll meet people who realised they were dreaming, and answered questions from inside the dream.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore

Why dreams can happen outside it
What your brain is doing while you dream
Why the strangeness never strikes you
The theories of why we dream
People who knew they were dreaming
Why dreams fade when you wake

segments.say: So let's begin with the question that sits underneath all of it. It sounds simple, and it's one of the oldest questions people have asked about their own minds. Why does a dream feel exactly like being awake?

Think about how odd this is. In a dream, you have no screen, no stage and no actors. Your eyes are closed, the room is dark and the outside world has been switched down to a murmur. And yet your mind produces a place so detailed that you can walk through it, talk to people in it, and be frightened by it. Whatever is going on, it is far more than a loose daydream.

Almost everyone dreams, whether they remember it or not. Some people wake with a vivid story every morning, and some say they hardly ever recall one. But the brain doesn't seem to take the night off. When we're asleep, it goes on working, quietly rearranging and replaying and imagining, and a dream is what that work looks like from the inside.

There's a second puzzle hiding inside the first. Most dreams are gone within minutes of waking. You can hold a scene in your mind at breakfast, and by lunchtime there's only the faintest shape of it left. If dreams are so vivid, why do they slip away so fast? We'll come to that near the end of the night, and the answer is rather beautiful.

Let's break the puzzle into three parts. First, why does a dream look and sound so real, with colours, faces and places that seem solid? Second, why doesn't the weirdness bother you, when a house turns into a school and your old friend is somehow also your neighbour? And third, why do you believe it completely, right up to the moment you wake? Each of these has a surprisingly good partial answer, and we'll collect them one by one.

Before we start, a quiet promise. Dream science is a young field, and it is full of open questions. Where there's a solid result, I'll tell you who found it and when it was published. Where researchers still disagree, I'll say so. You don't need to take anything on trust, and you don't need to leave with a neat answer. You only need to be curious.

Think of the quiet hours of the night. The street is still, the house is settled, and a single lamp is the only light in the room. From outside, it looks as though nothing is happening. But for a person asleep in that house, the most vivid scenes of the day may be playing out right now, with no light and no sound at all.

Let me set the scene for what scientists once believed. For most of history, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. You went to bed, the lights went out, and in the morning they came back on. The idea that something rich and active happens in between is a surprisingly recent one.

For a long time, people took it for granted that the sleeping brain was resting in much the same way that a tired muscle rests. Dreams were thought of as a kind of passing noise, or a message from somewhere else, depending on who you asked. What nobody had done was to watch a sleeping person through the whole night, and see what their body and brain were really up to.

When researchers finally did, in the middle of the twentieth century, they noticed something that took them by surprise. At certain moments in the night, a sleeper's eyes began to dart about under the closed lids, rapidly and in jerks, as if the person were watching something. The brain waves looked less like deep rest and more like waking. And when the sleeper was woken at those moments, the stories came pouring out. We'll meet that discovery properly in a moment.

For now, here is an idea to carry with you, because we'll come back to it. When you're dreaming, your brain may not be doing something wholly different from what it does when you're awake. It may be doing very much the same kind of work, building a model of a world and then living inside that model, only with the doors to the outside world mostly closed. Keep that thought nearby. By the middle of the night, it will start to make sense.

You might wonder why any of this is worth an evening. Dreams can seem trivial once the morning comes, a story that melts before breakfast. But they sit close to some of the largest questions about the mind. How does the brain create the feeling of a world? How does it know the difference between what is happening and what is only imagined? And what happens to those abilities when we sleep?

Dreams offer a rare window onto these questions. They show us the brain building a world without being told what to build. They show how memory and imagination blend, and how the line we usually take for granted between real and imagined can quietly fade. So when we ask why dreams feel real, we're also asking how waking life feels real, and that's a good deal more interesting than it first appears.

show.title: What dreams can tell us
items: How the brain builds a world
How we tell real from imagined

segments.say: There's something comforting about all this, too. People have dreamed for as long as there have been people, in every country, in every century. A farmer, a sailor and a child in the same village would have woken, from time to time, with a racing heart over something that never was. When you do it tonight, you're joining a very long line of dreamers.

Because the experience is so universal, people have always tried to explain it. Some saw dreams as visits from gods or ancestors. Some saw them as warnings, and some as simple nonsense. These ideas were thoughtful attempts to make sense of a puzzling thing, and they show how seriously people have always taken what happens in the dark.

Each of these answers tells us something about the people who gave it. If you believed that the night could carry a message, you would pay attention to your dreams, and write them down. If you believed that dreams were noise, you would shrug and carry on. Either way, the experience itself was never in doubt. Everyone agreed that it felt real, and that is the thing we are trying to explain.

show.title: Old answers to an old question

segments.say: Not every dream is a pleasant one, of course. Many of us have woken with the ache of losing someone, or the sting of an argument that never happened. And those feelings can linger into the morning, colouring the whole day. That, too, is part of what we mean when we say a dream feels real. The feeling is real, even when the story is not.

So how will we find our way through? We'll follow the order in which the science itself unfolded. First came the discovery of a new kind of sleep, then the surprise that dreams do not belong to that sleep alone, and then a series of experiments that opened up the dreaming brain piece by piece.

Along the way, you'll meet some wonderful pieces of research. A scientist who spent nights watching the closed eyes of a sleeper. Brain scans taken while people dreamed. Volunteers who were disturbed in small ways as they slept, to see whether the outside world would show up in their dreams. And people who learned to send a signal from inside a dream, with a movement of the eyes, to say that they knew where they were.

If your eyelids are getting heavy already, that's no problem. This video is made to be listened to in the dark, and by the end it slows down on purpose. You can listen with your eyes closed, you can let the details wash past, and you can wake up tomorrow with only the feeling that you learned something kind about your own mind.

Let's go back, then, to that first moment of waking, with your heart pounding over something that never happened. You were not foolish to believe it, and you were not broken for feeling it. Your brain was doing exactly what it has evolved to do, and it was doing it so well that you couldn't tell the difference. The question is how it pulls that off.

Here are four small questions to carry in your pocket for the rest of the night. Why does it look real? Why do I believe it? Why do I forget it by lunchtime? And why do I lie so still while my mind runs through a story? None of them has a one line answer, but each of them has a fascinating one.

One last thing before we begin. Let the facts come and go like cars passing on a distant road. What matters is the shape of the story, and the sense that your own mind, for all its strangeness, is something you can be curious about and kind to.

So, if you're comfortable, let's step back to the beginning. It's the early 1950s, in a university laboratory in Chicago, and a young researcher has set up a strange machine in the middle of the night. He's watching a pen draw a line on a moving roll of paper, and something about that line is not what he expected at all.
